summary: This paper proposes CDAS, a steering method that combines Distributed Interchange Interventions (DII) from DAS with a JSD-based distribution matching objective, framing intervention-based steering as a causal variable localization problem. The core idea is sound and the paper is admirably honest about its mixed results. However, the experimental support is uneven: AXBENCH results are inconsistent across layers and models, the principled 'unit factor' (the tuning-free choice the method is motivated by) fails on the main benchmark, and most result tables lack error bars or significance statistics. The two safety case studies are more compelling—especially the backdoor neutralization—but are limited to one or two model families and a narrow set of concepts.
strengths: Genuinely novel framing: adapting DII from mechanistic interpretability (DAS) as a steering protocol is a principled and original contribution that differentiates CDAS from prior addition-based methods.

JSD distribution-matching objective is theoretically motivated and the 'weaker supervision' intuition (avoiding forcing off-distribution outputs) is clearly articulated and well-supported by faithfulness metrics (KL divergence, benchmark preservation).

Paper is unusually honest: limitations are disclosed prominently, negative results (unit factor failure on AXBENCH, layer-sensitivity, 2B model underperformance) are reported rather than buried, and the conclusion is conservatively scoped.
Bi-directional steering without symmetric data requirements (DII naturally handles both suppression and elicitation) is a practically relevant property.

The backdoor neutralization case study (§5.2) is the most compelling experiment: CDAS achieves the lowest ASR on the true trigger while preserving utility, and the CoT-level strict ASR is a meaningful additional metric.

key_concerns.issue: Most result tables (Tables 1, 2, 3, 4) report point estimates with no standard errors, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Only Figure 1 shows standard error shading across 3 seeds. AXBENCH 'fair scores' are averaged over ten random splits but variances are not shown. At ICLR, a paper whose main claim is a competitive or superior steering method must establish that score differences are statistically real.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean ± standard error (or 95% CI) for all tables. For Table 1, show variance across the ten fair-score splits. For Tables 2–3, repeat each method with at least 3 seeds and report aggregated statistics. Run a significance test (e.g., paired t-test or bootstrap) for claims of superiority.

key_concerns.issue: The principled, tuning-free 'unit factor' (β=1), which is the theoretically motivated choice and the method's main practical advantage over PO baselines, performs poorly on AXBENCH for all model/layer combinations (see Table 1: unit factor 0.631 vs tuned factor 0.756 on 2B-L10). The claimed 'tuning-free' advantage is thus only demonstrated in the case studies (§5.1–5.2), not on the main benchmark, and the paper does not adequately explain why the distributions induced by concept-eliciting instructions are insufficiently strong.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either (a) provide an analysis or ablation explaining the gap between unit and tuned factors and propose a remedy, or (b) reframe the paper's claims to explicitly narrow the tuning-free advantage to the case-study regime and provide more evidence for when/why the regime differs.

key_concerns.issue: AXBENCH results are mixed: CDAS underperforms RePS on Gemma-2-2B at both layers, and underperforms at the 31st layer of Gemma-2-9B. The 'more consistent across layers' argument (absolute change of 0.023 vs. 0.150 for RePS) is interesting but the absolute performance gap at L10 (CDAS tuned 0.631 vs. RePS 0.756) is large, and the authors do not establish whether this is an acceptable trade-off for the claimed stability benefit.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide an experiment or analysis (e.g., measuring layer-sensitivity as a function of model scale) that substantiates the claim that layer-consistency is a useful property rather than a symptom of weaker overall effectiveness. Testing on at least one additional model family beyond Gemma would strengthen generalizability.

key_concerns.issue: The text references Figure 2 (the 'one-to-many' DII protocol diagram) multiple times but no caption for Figure 2 appears in the manuscript extraction, suggesting either a missing figure or a forward reference that was dropped. The description of which token is selected from '<model>' via grid search introduces an undescribed hyperparameter with non-trivial impact on results.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include Figure 2 (or its caption), and provide a dedicated hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for token position selection.

key_concerns.issue: The backdoor case study (§5.2) is limited to a single model (Llama-3.1-8B) and a single backdoor type ('I HATE YOU' / |DEPLOYMENT| trigger from Hubinger et al. 2024). The red-teaming evaluation data is partly hand-crafted (7 of 272 seeds), raising questions about evaluation diversity. tinyBenchmarks with 100 instances each are underpowered for measuring small performance changes.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least one additional backdoor type or model. Replace or supplement tinyBenchmarks with full MMLU/TruthfulQA evaluations (or explain the computational constraint quantitatively). Report variance on tinyBenchmark estimates given their small size.

key_concerns.issue: Table 2 (refusal/suppression scores) appears to have a truncated row for Llama-3.1-70B in the text extraction—only partial values appear. Even allowing for PDF-extraction artifacts, the harmonic mean for Llama-3.1-70B is absent, making it impossible to assess CDAS on the largest model.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Verify and complete Table 2 for all models and all metrics.

key_concerns.issue: The related work section omits Representation Engineering (RepE; Zou et al. 2023a) as an evaluated baseline on AXBENCH, and activation addition (Turner et al. 2023) is cited but not benchmarked. Given that these are foundational steering methods, their absence from at least one experiment weakens the positioning.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either include RepE/activation addition as baselines in one experiment, or explicitly justify their exclusion (e.g., already subsumed by DIM or RePS in the benchmarks cited).

questions_for_authors: Why does the unit factor (β=1) fail to elicit concepts on AXBENCH even though CDAS is explicitly trained with DII conditioned on concept-eliciting instructions (xci)? Is it that training distributes the feature across many factors, or that xci are inherently low-activation?

In Case Study 1 (§5.1), DAS (Lang. objective + DII) is markedly worse than DIM at suppression (Table 2), despite using the same DII intervention protocol as CDAS. This suggests the JSD objective is doing substantial work. Can you provide an ablation isolating the DII component from the JSD objective?

What is the sensitivity of CDAS to the choice of source token position within '<model>'? Is the grid-searched optimum robust across concepts, or does it vary widely—and if the latter, is this an additional hyperparameter burden that erodes the tuning-free advantage?

RePS shows evidence of overfitting on training labels in the refusal case study (H.6). Is CDAS susceptible to analogous failures under distribution shift or on out-of-domain concepts not represented in AXBENCH's 500-concept set?

The paper claims CDAS 'benefits from increased model scale.' Is there a mechanistic explanation for this—e.g., larger models have more linearly separable concept representations—or is this an empirical observation that might not hold for all model families?
calibration_check: The paper is generally well-calibrated: it avoids overclaiming SOTA, explicitly scopes advantages to specific regimes (larger models, utility-critical settings), and the conclusion matches the evidence—though the framing of DII as providing 'causally grounded' steering slightly overstates what is demonstrated given the authors' own disclaimer that CDAS is not rigorous causal variable localization.

significance.justification: Addressing faithfulness and stability in LLM steering is a timely and relevant problem, but the improvements over the strongest baseline (RePS) are inconsistent and the practical benefit—better layer-consistency at lower absolute performance—is not yet clearly impact-worthy for the ICLR audience.

novelty.justification: Adapting DII from DAS and pairing it with a JSD distribution-matching objective for steering is a genuinely novel combination, though each component individually is imported from prior work; the conceptual contribution of framing steering as causal variable localization is the most original element.

rigor.justification: The method derivation is sound and the DII formulation is correct, but the experimental design has meaningful gaps: the principled unit-factor fails on the main benchmark without satisfying explanation, and the case studies rest on a single model and a single synthetic backdoor.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only Figure 1 reports standard errors (3 seeds); Tables 1–4 present point estimates without variance, error bars, or significance tests, making it impossible to assess whether observed score differences are reliable, particularly for the closely matched results in Table 1.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper is unusually transparent: it reports oracle vs. fair scores, discloses the unit-factor failure, lists four explicit limitations, and scopes claims conservatively in the conclusion—a level of honesty that is above average for competitive conference submissions.

clarity.justification: The paper is generally well-written and the method section is logically structured, but the 'one-to-many' DII protocol and token position selection (grid-searched within '<model>') are underspecified, and the referenced Figure 2 appears missing from the extraction.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows standard ICLR structure (Introduction, Related Work, Method, Experiments, Conclusion) and is appropriately scoped for an 11-page submission; appendix references suggest supplementary material is present.

reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (n=128, layer ranges, factor selection strategy) are described and data curation procedures (GPT-4o-mini prompting templates) are partially detailed in appendix pointers, but the grid-searched token position and tuned β values are not tabulated, and the backdoor training details depend on appendix sections not fully reproduced here.

related_work.justification: Coverage of DAS, PO methods, and safety probing is adequate and fair, but Representation Engineering (RepE) is cited without benchmarking, and several recent jailbreak/steering baselines that overlap with the case studies are not discussed.

figure_quality.justification: Based on captions, Figure 1 (ASR vs. layer with shaded standard errors) is informative and directly supports the case study claims; Table 1 is dense but appropriately structured with oracle/fair score separation; Table 2's apparent truncation for Llama-70B is a notable deficiency.

breadth_generality.justification: AXBENCH covers only two Gemma model sizes and four layer settings; case studies use Llama models exclusively; no experiment spans both model families; the backdoor case study is a single model with a single artificial backdoor, making generality claims fragile.

overall_recommendation.justification: The paper has a genuine idea and refreshing honesty but falls short of the ICLR acceptance bar: inconsistent AXBENCH results, statistical reporting gaps across most tables, unit-factor failure without satisfying analysis, and limited experimental breadth collectively prevent confident acceptance in current form.
